lines.title: Will your money last?
lines.intro: You start with ₹20,000 in the festival fund. On each date, the bills you signed are paid out of it. The bar shows how much money is still in the fund after that date's bills.
lines.promised: Could be {{money}} if every promise arrives
lines.keySure: Money you are sure of (your ₹20,000 minus bills)
lines.keyPromised: Plus promised money (sponsor, donation, ticket sales). It may not come.
lines.explainOk: Spare money is what is left over when it is tightest ({{when}}), counting only sure money. Surprise bills of ₹500 to ₹2,000 will come out of it. The more you keep, the safer you are.
lines.explainShort: You would not have enough sure money to pay that date's bills. Take something out, pick a cheaper offer, or pay later.
lines.note: Bills counted are the ones you signed, plus permits. Surprise bills are not counted yet. On Festival Day we also count the event money you expect.

L1.what: In {{when}} you needed {{due}} and had {{cash}}. The sponsor came after the deadline.
L1.ok: Every bill was paid from cash you had in hand, on its date.
L1.idea: Money you expect is not money you have. A bill is paid from cash in hand on its date.

more.what: Money you expect can arrive later than the bill that needs it. Week 3 is where that gap shows.
more.idea: A promise is not cash. Bills are due on a date, whoever still owes you.
more.example: A club is promised ₹10,000 on the 20th, but its ₹6,000 tent is due on the 15th. It has ₹2,000 on the 15th, so it cannot pay in full.
more.real: Shops and suppliers usually want payment on the due date. Planners list when money really arrives, not just how much.
more.ask: Which of my expected amounts is only a promise? What is due before it arrives?

L2.what: {{item}} was cancelled, so {{goal}} was not met.
L2.ok: Nothing was cancelled. Each goal had money for its job.
L2.idea: Every rupee has one job. Funding one goal makes another wait.

more.what: When cash ran short, something had to go, and the goal it served went with it. Ranking your goals decided what was protected.
more.idea: Money can only do one job at a time. Choosing a goal first makes the trade-off visible before the pressure comes.
more.example: Sana has ₹3,000. Lights and sound cost ₹3,000 and the kids' corner costs ₹3,000. Buying one means the other waits.
more.real: Families and clubs rank needs before a tight month. It is easier to choose calmly than in a rush.
more.ask: Which goal matters most to me? What am I giving up for it?

L3.what: The crowd was {{crowd}}; you ordered {{plates}}; {{n}} rush plates cost ₹45 each.
L3.extra: The crowd was {{crowd}}; you ordered {{plates}}; {{n}} unused plates were still paid.
L3.none: The crowd was {{crowd}} and there was no food order.
L3.idea: The hall cost the same for any crowd. Food grows with every visitor.
L3.rule: Know which costs move with the crowd.

more.what: Food grows with every visitor, but the hall costs the same either way. The crowd decided how many plates you needed.
more.idea: Fixed costs stay the same however many people come. Variable costs rise and fall with the crowd.
more.example: A stall pays ₹500 rent and ₹10 per snack. For 20 snacks it costs ₹700; for 40 snacks it costs ₹900. The rent never moved.
more.real: Rent and permits are fixed. Ingredients and packaging are variable.
more.ask: Which of my costs change with the number of people? Which stay the same?

L4.what: The Basic set showed {{quote}}. With required extras it cost {{total}}.
L4.skip: The Basic set showed {{quote}}. With required extras it would have cost {{total}}.
L4.idea: The quote is where the price starts. Add what is required, then compare totals.

more.what: The quote on the sign was not what the set really cost. A required extra was in the fine print.
more.idea: A quote is only where the price starts. Required extras change the real price, so compare totals.
more.example: Set A is ₹5,000 with everything included. Set B is ₹3,500 plus a ₹2,000 required fee. Set A is cheaper.
more.real: Delivery, setup and service charges can be added later. Ask what is required before you compare.
more.ask: What else do I have to pay to use this? What is the total?

L5.what: Your plan held in {{k}} of 10 possible festivals. It first broke on {{when}}: {{bill}}.
L5.all: Your plan held in all 10 possible festivals.
L5.idea: One late payment can break a plan that looked fine. Spare money should be sized by risks you can name.
L5.rule: Name the risks, then size your spare money.

more.what: Your plan was replayed in ten different festivals. The ones that broke show where the plan was thin.
more.idea: A late sponsor, a smaller crowd or a bigger repair bill can break a plan that looked fine. Spare money sized for risks you can name is a stress test passed in advance.
more.example: A stall plan fails in 4 of 10 imagined cases, all on the same date. Moving one payment off that date fixes it.
more.real: Planners ask "what if the money is late?" before it happens. They keep spare money for the risks they can name.
more.ask: What could go wrong on my tightest date? How much spare money would cover it?

L7.what: The Combo said "Was {{was}}". The same three things cost {{parts}} at Daam Fix.
L7.idea: A high "was" price, a bundle and a countdown make a price look small.

more.what: The Combo looked like a bargain next to a made-up higher price. The same parts at Daam Fix cost less.
more.idea: A high "was" price, a bundle and a countdown make a price look small. They make you decide before you check.
more.example: A jacket says "Was ₹4,000, now ₹2,000, ends today". The shop next door sells it for ₹1,800 every day.
more.real: Sales work best on things you had not planned to buy. Look up the normal price before the deal ends.
more.ask: What is the normal price? Would I buy this if it had no countdown?
